assessments.reasoning: The February 1963 preface names Manchester University Atlas and is signed by Brooker and Rohl. Printed I.3 explicitly names Atlas Autocode a language. The two pages together specify the source-language referent.

The March 1965 Manchester preface describes its own then-current compiler, signed by the same authors. It confirms continuity of the named project while the 1963 manual fixes the identity statement and the later compiler has its own applicability.

The Edinburgh cover identifies the October 1965 KDF9 compiler, and the June 1966 amendment distinguishes hardware and compiler variants. The scan establishes useful implementation boundaries and supplies no substitute authority for the Manchester 1963 language claim.

challenge.method: Compare the exact February 1963 and March 1965 Manchester manuals with the Edinburgh KDF9 cover and June 1966 amendment, then inspect the entire CHM section and nearby Atlas Algol heading.
challenge.results: The earliest manual in this packet distinguishes the language and machine. The 1965 Manchester compiler and Edinburgh port add dated contexts. The neighboring Atlas Algol heading, earlier Autocode entries and IMP provide differentiation.

limitations: The association is at generic Atlas Autocode language scope. No historical identity merge with earlier Autocodes, Atlas Algol, or KDF9 implementations was justified.
